claim: A polymorphism in the autophagy gene Atg16l1 is associated with susceptibility to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
source: A polymorphism in the autophagy gene Atg16l1 is associated with susceptibility to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Selective deletion of Atg16l1 in T cells in mice resulted in spontaneous intestinal inflammation.
source: Selective deletion of Atg16l1 in T cells in mice resulted in spontaneous intestinal inflammation that was characterized by aberrant type 2 responses to dietary and microbiota antigens, and by a loss of Foxp3+ Treg cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.

claim: Selective deletion of Atg16l1 in T cells resulted in aberrant type 2 responses to dietary and microbiota antigens.
source: Selective deletion of Atg16l1 in T cells in mice resulted in spontaneous intestinal inflammation that was characterized by aberrant type 2 responses to dietary and microbiota antigens, and by a loss of Foxp3+ Treg cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data showing elevated TH2 responses and antibodies to dietary and commensal antigens.

claim: Selective deletion of Atg16l1 in T cells resulted in a loss of Foxp3+ Treg cells.
source: Selective deletion of Atg16l1 in T cells in mice resulted in spontaneous intestinal inflammation that was characterized by aberrant type 2 responses to dietary and microbiota antigens, and by a loss of Foxp3+ Treg cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through flow cytometry data showing reduced Treg frequencies and numbers.

claim: Autophagy directly promotes Foxp3+ Treg cell survival in the intestine.
source: Specific ablation of Atg16l1 in Foxp3+ Treg cells in mice demonstrated that autophagy directly promotes their survival and metabolic adaptation in the intestine.
evidence: This is demonstrated through Treg-specific deletion experiments in Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice and survival assays.

claim: Autophagy promotes metabolic adaptation of Foxp3+ Treg cells in the intestine.
source: Specific ablation of Atg16l1 in Foxp3+ Treg cells in mice demonstrated that autophagy directly promotes their survival and metabolic adaptation in the intestine.
evidence: This is demonstrated through gene expression analysis showing altered metabolic profiles in autophagy-deficient Treg cells.

claim: Autophagy directly limits mucosal TH2 cell expansion.
source: Moreover, we also identify an unexpected role for autophagy in directly limiting mucosal TH2 cell expansion.
evidence: This is demonstrated through adoptive transfer experiments and in vitro survival assays showing cell-intrinsic effects.

claim: A single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in ATG16L1 was associated with an increased risk of Crohn's disease.
source: Among these, a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in the essential macroautophagy (hereafter called 'autophagy') gene ATG16L1 was associated with an increased risk of CD (Hampe et al., 2007; Rioux et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to GWAS studies.

claim: The IBD predisposing T300A mutation in ATG16L1 led to increased degradation of ATG16L1 protein and reduced autophagy.
source: A recent study showed that the IBD predisposing T300A mutation in the coding region of ATG16L1 led to increased degradation of ATG16L1 protein and reduced autophagy (Murthy et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Decreased autophagy may contribute to IBD development.
source: A recent study showed that the IBD predisposing T300A mutation in the coding region of ATG16L1 led to increased degradation of ATG16L1 protein and reduced autophagy (Murthy et al., 2014), indicating that decreased autophagy may contribute to IBD development.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited study on the T300A mutation.

claim: Polymorphisms in autophagy-related genes IRGM, LRRK2 and SMURF1 are linked to IBD susceptibility.
source: Polymorphisms in several other autophagy-related genes, including IRGM, LRRK2 and SMURF1, are also linked to IBD susceptibility (Van Limbergen et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review of genetic studies.

claim: Changes in the autophagy pathway alter intestinal homeostasis and predispose to chronic intestinal inflammation.
source: Polymorphisms in several other autophagy-related genes, including IRGM, LRRK2 and SMURF1, are also linked to IBD susceptibility (Van Limbergen et al., 2014), suggesting that changes in the autophagy pathway alter intestinal homeostasis and predispose to chronic intestinal inflammation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic association data.

claim: Atg16l1 forms an essential autophagy complex with Atg5 and Atg12 that facilitates elongation of the initial isolation membrane.
source: Atg16l1 forms an essential autophagy complex with Atg5 and Atg12 that facilitates elongation of the initial isolation membrane that results in engulfment of the cargo and formation of the autophagosome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the molecular function of Atg16l1 in autophagy.

claim: Atg16l1 plays a role in Paneth cell physiology.
source: In these studies, Atg16l1 was shown to play a role in Paneth cell physiology, as well as in bacterial handling and regulation of inflammatory IL-1β secretion by myeloid cells (Cadwell et al., 2008; Kuballa et al., 2008; Saitoh et al., 2008; Plantinga et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Atg16l1 plays a role in bacterial handling by myeloid cells.
source: In these studies, Atg16l1 was shown to play a role in Paneth cell physiology, as well as in bacterial handling and regulation of inflammatory IL-1β secretion by myeloid cells (Cadwell et al., 2008; Kuballa et al., 2008; Saitoh et al., 2008; Plantinga et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Atg16l1 plays a role in regulation of inflammatory IL-1β secretion by myeloid cells.
source: In these studies, Atg16l1 was shown to play a role in Paneth cell physiology, as well as in bacterial handling and regulation of inflammatory IL-1β secretion by myeloid cells (Cadwell et al., 2008; Kuballa et al., 2008; Saitoh et al., 2008; Plantinga et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CD4+ T cells constitute the largest population of intestinal lymphocytes.
source: CD4+ T cells constitute the largest population of intestinal lymphocytes and are central mediators of host protective and tolerogenic responses in the gut (Shale et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Foxp3+ CD4+ regulatory T cells are indispensable in promoting tolerance toward commensal and dietary antigens.
source: In particular, thymus-derived and peripherally induced Foxp3+ CD4+ regulatory T cells (tTreg and pTreg cells, respectively) are indispensable in promoting tolerance toward commensal and dietary antigens and for the prevention of aberrant effector T cell responses, including TH1, TH2 and TH17 cell responses (Izcue et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Foxp3+ CD4+ regulatory T cells are indispensable for the prevention of aberrant effector T cell responses.
source: In particular, thymus-derived and peripherally induced Foxp3+ CD4+ regulatory T cells (tTreg and pTreg cells, respectively) are indispensable in promoting tolerance toward commensal and dietary antigens and for the prevention of aberrant effector T cell responses, including TH1, TH2 and TH17 cell responses (Izcue et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: An imbalance between effector and regulatory CD4+ T cells can promote chronic intestinal inflammation.
source: An imbalance between effector and regulatory CD4+ T cells can promote chronic intestinal inflammation and accumulation of effector CD4+ T cells in the inflamed mucosa is a cardinal feature of IBD (Abraham and Cho, 2009; Maloy and Powrie, 2011; Shale et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Accumulation of effector CD4+ T cells in the inflamed mucosa is a cardinal feature of IBD.
source: An imbalance between effector and regulatory CD4+ T cells can promote chronic intestinal inflammation and accumulation of effector CD4+ T cells in the inflamed mucosa is a cardinal feature of IBD (Abraham and Cho, 2009; Maloy and Powrie, 2011; Shale et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mice with T-cell-specific deletion of essential autophagy genes exhibited decreased frequencies and numbers of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: Previous studies utilizing mice with T-cell-specific deletion of essential autophagy genes (Atg3, Atg5, Atg7, Beclin1) pointed to a key role of autophagy in T cell homeostasis, as these mice exhibited decreased frequencies and numbers of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and defects in T cell proliferation in vitro (Pua et al., 2009; Stephenson et al., 2009; Jia and He, 2011; Kovacs et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mice with T-cell-specific deletion of essential autophagy genes exhibited defects in T cell proliferation in vitro.
source: Previous studies utilizing mice with T-cell-specific deletion of essential autophagy genes (Atg3, Atg5, Atg7, Beclin1) pointed to a key role of autophagy in T cell homeostasis, as these mice exhibited decreased frequencies and numbers of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and defects in T cell proliferation in vitro (Pua et al., 2009; Stephenson et al., 2009; Jia and He, 2011; Kovacs et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Autophagy is important for the development of memory CD8+ T cells.
source: In addition, recent studies highlighted the importance of autophagy in the development of memory CD8+ T cells (Puleston et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2014; Schlie et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: CD4+ T cells isolated from control Atg16l1fl/fl mice exhibited increased LC3+ autophagosome formation after activation.
source: CD4+ T cells isolated from control Atg16l1fl/fl mice exhibited increased LC3+ autophagosome formation after activation, as measured by intracellular LC3 accumulation in the presence of a lysosomal inhibitor (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There was no increase in intracellular LC3 accumulation in CD4+ T cells from Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice after activation.
source: In contrast, there was no increase in intracellular LC3 accumulation in CD4+ T cells from Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Activated control Atg16l1fl/fl CD4+ T cells exhibited increased lipidated LC3 II levels in the presence of chloroquine.
source: Activated control Atg16l1fl/fl CD4+ T cells exhibited increased lipidated LC3 II levels in the presence of chloroquine, indicative of autophagy-mediated turnover of LC3 II after T cell activation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: LC3 II levels in CD4+ T cells from Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice were barely affected by activation.
source: However, LC3 II levels in CD4+ T cells from Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice were barely affected by activation (Figure 1B), confirming a block in autophagy.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice initially gained weight in a manner comparable to Atg16l1fl/fl littermates.
source: Young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice appeared normal, initially gained weight in a manner comparable to Atg16l1fl/fl littermates and exhibited normal intestinal morphology (Figure 1C,F-H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by weight curve data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice exhibited normal intestinal morphology.
source: Young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice appeared normal, initially gained weight in a manner comparable to Atg16l1fl/fl littermates and exhibited normal intestinal morphology (Figure 1C,F-H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological images shown in Figures 1F-H.

claim: From around 5 months of age, Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice stopped gaining weight.
source: However, from around 5 months of age, Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice stopped gaining weight (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by weight curve data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Aged Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice developed splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy.
source: However, from around 5 months of age, Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice stopped gaining weight (Figure 1C), developed splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy (Figure 1D,E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by images and spleen weight data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Aged Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice developed chronic intestinal pathology that progressed with age.
source: However, from around 5 months of age, Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice stopped gaining weight (Figure 1C), developed splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy (Figure 1D,E) and chronic intestinal pathology that progressed with age (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological data shown in Figures 1F-I.

claim: Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice exhibited significant inflammation of both the small intestine and colon.
source: Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice exhibited significant inflammation of both the small intestine (SI) and colon, characterized by increased SI length, marked lengthening of crypts, shortening of villi and epithelial hyperplasia (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological and morphometric data shown in Figures 1F-I.

claim: Thymic T cell production was unperturbed in Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: Whilst thymic T cell production was unperturbed in Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data of thymic populations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Frequencies of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in peripheral lymphoid organs were significantly decreased in Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice compared to Atg16l1fl/fl littermates.
source: frequencies of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in peripheral lymphoid organs were significantly decreased compared to Atg16l1fl/fl littermates (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Significant decreases in intestinal T cell frequencies and numbers were observed in the cLP and SI LP of Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: Furthermore, we observed significant decreases in intestinal T cell frequencies and numbers in the cLP and SI LP of Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Frequencies of colonic TH1 and TH17 populations were comparable in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice and Atg16l1fl/fl littermates.
source: Analysis of the effector CD4+ T cell compartment in Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice revealed that frequencies of colonic TH1 (IFN-γ+) and TH17 (IL-17A+) populations were comparable in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice and Atg16l1fl/fl littermates (Figure 2B,D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2B and 2D.

claim: Total TH1 and TH17 numbers were significantly decreased in Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: although, due to decreased colonic CD4+ T cell numbers, total TH1 and TH17 numbers were significantly decreased (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell count data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Both frequencies and total numbers of TH2 cells were significantly increased in cLP of young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: Conversely, both frequencies and total numbers of TH2 (IL-13+) cells were significantly increased in cLP of young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2B-D.

claim: IL-13-producing cells in Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice were bona fide TH2 cells that co-expressed Gata3.
source: These IL-13-producing cells were bona fide TH2 cells, as they co-expressed the lineage-specifying transcription factor Gata3 (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data showing co-expression of IL-13 and Gata3 in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: TH2 cell accumulation was primarily observed in the intestinal mucosa of Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: Interestingly, TH2 cell accumulation was primarily observed in the intestinal mucosa of Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice, as TH2 cell frequencies were only marginally increased in the mLN and remained unchanged in the spleen (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data comparing different tissues shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice had increased frequencies of eosinophils in both the spleen and mLN.
source: However, the functional consequences of TH2 expansion extended beyond the intestine, as Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice had increased frequencies of eosinophils in both the spleen and mLN and elevated serum levels of mast cell protease 1 (MCPT-1), a marker of intestinal mast cell activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice had elevated serum levels of mast cell protease 1 (MCPT-1).
source: However, the functional consequences of TH2 expansion extended beyond the intestine, as Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice had increased frequencies of eosinophils in both the spleen and mLN and elevated serum levels of mast cell protease 1 (MCPT-1), a marker of intestinal mast cell activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The frequencies of intestinal Foxp3+ Treg cells in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice were severely reduced in both the SI and cLP.
source: Indeed, we found that the frequencies of intestinal Foxp3+ Treg cells in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice were severely reduced, both in the SI and cLP (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2F and 2G.

claim: Treg cell numbers were reduced by around 10-fold in the colonic LP and 4-fold in SI LP of Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: Taking into account the decreased frequencies of CD4+ T cells in Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice (Figure 2A), this equated to a reduction in Treg cell numbers by around 10-fold in the colonic LP and 4-fold in SI LP (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is calculated from flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Thymic development of Foxp3+ Treg cells was not diminished in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: In contrast, thymic development of Foxp3+ Treg cells was not diminished in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data of thymic Treg cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Minor but significant reductions in the frequencies and absolute numbers of Foxp3+ Treg cells were observed in the spleen and mLN of Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: and we observed only minor, though significant, reductions in the frequencies and absolute numbers of Foxp3+ Treg cells in the spleen and mLN of Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice compared with Atg16l1fl/fl littermates (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Atg16l1-deficiency profoundly affected the maintenance of Foxp3+ Treg cells in the periphery, particularly within the intestinal mucosa.
source: Thus, Atg16l1-deficiency profoundly affected the maintenance of Foxp3+ Treg cells in the periphery, particularly within the intestinal mucosa.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing differential effects on Treg cells in different tissues.

claim: Expression of neuropilin-1 (Nrp1) and Helios were found at comparable levels on intestinal Foxp3+ Treg cells from Atg16l1fl/fl and Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: Expression of neuropilin-1 (Nrp1) and Helios, putative markers proposed to distinguish pTreg and tTreg cells, were found at comparable levels on intestinal Foxp3+ Treg cells from Atg16l1fl/fl and Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice, suggesting that the local environment, rather than site of Treg induction, primarily dictates the requirement for autophagy in Treg cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C,D.

claim: The local environment, rather than site of Treg induction, primarily dictates the requirement for autophagy in Treg cells.
source: Expression of neuropilin-1 (Nrp1) and Helios, putative markers proposed to distinguish pTreg and tTreg cells, were found at comparable levels on intestinal Foxp3+ Treg cells from Atg16l1fl/fl and Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice, suggesting that the local environment, rather than site of Treg induction, primarily dictates the requirement for autophagy in Treg cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C,D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparable expression of tTreg and pTreg markers.

claim: Impaired autophagy significantly increased expression of effector TH cytokines in Treg cells from cLP and SI LP.
source: Assessment of how Atg16l1-deficiency affected intestinal Foxp3+ Treg cell phenotype showed that impaired autophagy significantly increased expression of effector TH cytokines in Treg cells from cLP and SI LP (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4E.

claim: cLP Treg cells from young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice showed higher expression of CD103 and CTLA-4.
source: We also found that cLP Treg cells from young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice showed higher expression of CD103 and CTLA-4, but showed decreased expression of the activation markers CD25, CD69, and the terminal differentiation marker KLRG-1 (Cheng et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4F.

claim: cLP Treg cells from young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice showed decreased expression of CD25, CD69, and KLRG-1.
source: We also found that cLP Treg cells from young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice showed higher expression of CD103 and CTLA-4, but showed decreased expression of the activation markers CD25, CD69, and the terminal differentiation marker KLRG-1 (Cheng et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4F.

claim: Intestinal Treg cells from young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice had significantly increased expression of Ki67.
source: In addition, intestinal Treg cells from young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice had significantly increased expression of Ki67 and higher levels of phosphorylated S6, suggesting that the majority were in cell cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 4G–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4G-I.

claim: Intestinal Treg cells from young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice had higher levels of phosphorylated S6.
source: In addition, intestinal Treg cells from young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice had significantly increased expression of Ki67 and higher levels of phosphorylated S6, suggesting that the majority were in cell cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 4G–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4G-I.

claim: Autophagy plays an integral role in the maintenance and functional regulation of intestinal Treg cells.
source: Taken together, these results identify a crucial role for autophagy in the maintenance and functional regulation of intestinal Treg cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multiple phenotypic and functional changes observed in autophagy-deficient Treg cells.

claim: Serum IgE concentrations were significantly elevated in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: While at the limit of detection in Atg16l1fl/fl controls, serum IgE concentrations were significantly elevated in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice and increased further as the mice aged (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Serum IgE concentrations increased further as Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice aged.
source: While at the limit of detection in Atg16l1fl/fl controls, serum IgE concentrations were significantly elevated in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice and increased further as the mice aged (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Levels of serum IgA and IgG1 in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice were significantly elevated relative to Atg16l1fl/fl littermates.
source: Furthermore, levels of serum IgA and IgG1 in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice were also significantly elevated relative to Atg16l1fl/fl littermates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and again increased as the Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice aged (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3B.

claim: Levels of isotypes not associated with TH2 help were identical in aged Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice and Atg16l1fl/fl littermates.
source: In contrast, levels of isotypes not associated with TH2 help were identical in aged Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice and Atg16l1fl/fl littermates (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a progressive dysregulation of TH2-associated antibody responses in Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: Thus, there was a progressive dysregulation of TH2-associated antibody responses in Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the progressive increase in TH2-associated antibody isotypes.

claim: Young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice had higher frequencies of germinal center, memory B cells and plasma cells in the spleen and mLN compared to Atg16l1fl/fl littermates.
source: Consistent with these elevated humoral responses, young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice had higher frequencies of germinal center (GC), memory B cells and plasma cells in the spleen and mLN compared to Atg16l1fl/fl littermates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Markedly enlarged Peyer's patches were observed in aged Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: and markedly enlarged Peyer's patches were observed in aged Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological images shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Aged Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice had high levels of anti-soy IgG1 and IgA in sera.
source: Soy is the main protein source in chow, and we detected high levels of anti-soy IgG1 and IgA in sera from aged Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice, whereas these responses were undetectable in control Atg16l1fl/fl littermates (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Anti-soy antibody responses were undetectable in control Atg16l1fl/fl littermates.
source: Soy is the main protein source in chow, and we detected high levels of anti-soy IgG1 and IgA in sera from aged Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice, whereas these responses were undetectable in control Atg16l1fl/fl littermates (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Only marginal levels of soy-specific IgG2b or IgG2c were detected in aged Atg16l1ΔCD4 sera.
source: By contrast, we only detected marginal levels of soy-specific IgG2b or IgG2c in aged Atg16l1ΔCD4 sera (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Elevated anti-soy IgG1 and IgA antibodies were already present in sera from young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice, before the onset of intestinal inflammation.
source: Importantly, elevated anti-soy IgG1 and IgA antibodies were already present in sera from young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice, before the onset of intestinal inflammation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice exhibited significantly elevated levels of anti-OVA IgE after being fed OVA alone.
source: In contrast, Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice exhibited significantly elevated levels of anti-OVA IgE after being fed OVA alone and developed >10-fold higher levels of OVA-specific IgE after feeding of OVA with CT (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice developed >10-fold higher levels of OVA-specific IgE after feeding of OVA with cholera toxin.
source: In contrast, Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice exhibited significantly elevated levels of anti-OVA IgE after being fed OVA alone and developed >10-fold higher levels of OVA-specific IgE after feeding of OVA with CT (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice displayed aberrant TH2-associated antibody responses towards otherwise innocuous dietary protein antigens.
source: Together, these results indicate that Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice displayed aberrant TH2-associated antibody responses towards otherwise innocuous dietary protein antigens.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on anti-soy and anti-OVA antibody responses.

claim: Significantly higher levels of CBir1-specific IgG1 and IgA were detected in the serum of aged Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice compared to control Atg16l1fl/fl littermates.
source: We detected significantly higher levels of CBir1-specific IgG1 and IgA in the serum of aged Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice compared to control Atg16l1fl/fl littermates, whereas anti-CBir1 IgG2b and IgG2c levels were comparable (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Anti-CBir1 IgG2b and IgG2c levels were comparable between aged Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice and control Atg16l1fl/fl littermates.
source: We detected significantly higher levels of CBir1-specific IgG1 and IgA in the serum of aged Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice compared to control Atg16l1fl/fl littermates, whereas anti-CBir1 IgG2b and IgG2c levels were comparable (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CBir1-specific IgG1 and IgA were already detectable in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: Furthermore, CBir1-specific IgG1 and IgA were already detectable in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text but data are not shown.

claim: Increased TH2 cell-associated antibody responses were not mounted in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice following oral infection with Helicobacter hepaticus.
source: In contrast, increased TH2 cell-associated antibody responses were not mounted in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice following oral infection either with the Gram-negative bacterium Helicobacter hepaticus or with the nematode parasite Trichuris muris (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Increased TH2 cell-associated antibody responses were not mounted in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice following oral infection with Trichuris muris.
source: In contrast, increased TH2 cell-associated antibody responses were not mounted in young Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice following oral infection either with the Gram-negative bacterium Helicobacter hepaticus or with the nematode parasite Trichuris muris (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: The abnormal TH2-associated antibody responses observed in Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice preceded the development of overt inflammation.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the abnormal TH2-associated antibody responses observed in Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice preceded the development of overt inflammation and were selectively induced towards commensal microbiota and dietary antigens.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of elevated antibodies in young mice before pathology onset.

claim: The abnormal TH2-associated antibody responses in Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice were selectively induced towards commensal microbiota and dietary antigens.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the abnormal TH2-associated antibody responses observed in Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice preceded the development of overt inflammation and were selectively induced towards commensal microbiota and dietary antigens.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the selective responses to soy and CBir1 but not to pathogens.

claim: Under TH2 or Treg polarizing conditions, differentiation of naïve CD4+ T cells isolated from Atg16l1ΔCD4 or Atg16l1fl/fl littermates toward the Gata3+ TH2 or Foxp3+ Treg cell phenotype was comparable.
source: We found that, under TH2 or Treg polarizing conditions, differentiation of naïve CD4+ T cells isolated from Atg16l1ΔCD4 or Atg16l1fl/fl littermates toward the Gata3+ TH2 or Foxp3+ Treg cell phenotype was comparable (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro differentiation assays shown in Figures 4A-C.

claim: No evidence of Treg instability was found when Foxp3+ Treg cells were activated in the presence of IL-4 and IL-13.
source: However, we did not find any evidence of Treg instability, as expression of Foxp3 and CD25 remained equally high in Atg16l1-deficient and WT Treg cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Atg16l1-deficient TH2 cells exhibited comparable or improved survival relative to WT TH2 cells following activation with different concentrations of anti-CD3 antibody.
source: Following activation with different concentrations of anti-CD3 antibody, Atg16l1-deficient TH2 cells exhibited comparable or improved survival relative to WT TH2 cells (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro survival assays shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: There was a 50–75% decrease in survival of Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells when compared to Atg16l1-sufficient Treg cells activated under the same conditions.
source: In contrast, there was a 50–75% decrease in survival of Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells when compared to Atg16l1-sufficient Treg cells activated under the same conditions (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro survival assays shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: An increased proportion of Atg16l1-deficient intestinal Treg cells were dead or dying compared to WT Treg cells.
source: We observed that an increased proportion of Atg16l1-deficient intestinal Treg cells were dead or dying compared to WT Treg cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Annexin V staining shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Atg16l1-deficiency had no negative effect on the viability of intestinal TH2 cells.
source: In contrast, Atg16l1-deficiency had no negative effect on the viability of intestinal TH2 cells, which was comparable to WT controls (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Annexin V staining shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Atg16l1-deficiency does not impair the differentiation or stability of Treg cells.
source: Together, these results indicate that Atg16l1-deficiency does not impair the differentiation or stability of Treg cells and does not promote differentiation towards the TH2 lineage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro differentiation and stability assays.

claim: Atg16l1-deficiency does not promote differentiation towards the TH2 lineage.
source: Together, these results indicate that Atg16l1-deficiency does not impair the differentiation or stability of Treg cells and does not promote differentiation towards the TH2 lineage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro differentiation assays.

claim: Autophagy differentially impacts on the survival of mucosal Treg and TH2 cells.
source: However, autophagy differentially impacts on the survival of mucosal Treg and TH2 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential survival effects observed in vitro and in vivo.

claim: Donor WT CD4+ T cells accounted for 37 ± 5% of total CD4+ T cells in spleen, 18 ± 2% in mLN, and 56 ± 4% in cLP of reconstituted Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: In reconstituted Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice, donor WT CD4+ T cells accounted for 37 ± 5% of total CD4+ T cells in spleen and 18 ± 2% in mLN, whereas in the cLP they represented 56 ± 4% (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data from adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Autophagy-deficient CD4+ T cells had a survival disadvantage when compared to WT CD4+ T cells within the intestinal mucosa.
source: Thus, autophagy-deficient CD4+ T cells had a survival disadvantage when compared to WT CD4+ T cells within the intestinal mucosa.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential reconstitution of WT vs Atg16l1-deficient cells in different tissues.

claim: Around 50% of the donor WT naïve CD45.1+ T cells developed into Foxp3+ pTreg cells in spleen, mLN and cLP of Atg16l1ΔCD4 recipients.
source: When we examined Foxp3+ Treg cells, the survival advantage conferred by autophagy was even more apparent, with around 50% of the donor WT naïve CD45.1+ T cells developing into Foxp3+ pTreg cells in spleen, mLN and cLP of Atg16l1ΔCD4 recipients.
evidence: This is stated based on flow cytometry data from adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: The majority of Foxp3+ Treg cells in reconstituted Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice were of WT donor origin (67 ± 5% in spleen, 59 ± 4% in mLN and 80 ± 5% in cLP).
source: As a result, the majority of Foxp3+ Treg cells were of WT donor origin (67 ± 5% in spleen, 59 ± 4% in mLN and 80 ± 5% in cLP) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data from adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Significantly higher frequencies of Gata3+ IL-13+ TH2 cells were observed among Atg16l1-deficient CD45.2+ CD4+ T cells compared with the WT donor CD45.1+ CD4+ T cells in the cLP of reconstituted Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: When we analyzed the frequencies of TH2 cells in the cLP of reconstituted Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice, we observed significantly higher frequencies of Gata3+ IL-13+ TH2 cells among Atg16l1-deficient CD45.2+ CD4+ T cells compared with the WT donor CD45.1+ CD4+ T cells (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data from adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figures 5C-E.

claim: Frequencies of IL-13+ Atg16l1-deficient CD4+ T cells in the cLP of pTreg-reconstituted mice were comparable to those found in untreated Atg16l1ΔCD4 littermates.
source: Indeed, frequencies of IL-13+ Atg16l1-deficient CD4+ T cells in the cLP of pTreg-reconstituted mice were comparable to those found in untreated Atg16l1ΔCD4 littermates (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data comparing reconstituted and untreated mice shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: There was no difference in TH17 cell frequencies between Atg16l1-deficient CD45.2+ and WT CD4+ T cells in reconstituted mice.
source: In contrast, there was no difference in TH17 cell frequencies between Atg16l1-deficient CD45.2+ and WT CD4+ T cells, and there was a significant decrease in TH1 frequencies among Atg16l1-deficient CD4+ T cells (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data from adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: There was a significant decrease in TH1 frequencies among Atg16l1-deficient CD4+ T cells in reconstituted mice.
source: In contrast, there was no difference in TH17 cell frequencies between Atg16l1-deficient CD45.2+ and WT CD4+ T cells, and there was a significant decrease in TH1 frequencies among Atg16l1-deficient CD4+ T cells (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data from adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Provision of WT pTreg cells did not rescue the increased TH2 phenotype of Atg16l1-deficient CD4+ T cells.
source: Thus, provision of WT pTreg cells did not rescue the increased TH2 phenotype of Atg16l1-deficient CD4+ T cells, indicating that autophagy directly regulates TH2 cells through a cell-intrinsic mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the adoptive transfer experiments showing persistent TH2 expansion despite Treg reconstitution.

claim: Autophagy directly regulates TH2 cells through a cell-intrinsic mechanism.
source: Thus, provision of WT pTreg cells did not rescue the increased TH2 phenotype of Atg16l1-deficient CD4+ T cells, indicating that autophagy directly regulates TH2 cells through a cell-intrinsic mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice reconstituted with WT pTreg cells still developed intestinal pathology comparable to untreated Atg16l1ΔCD4 littermates.
source: Consistent with this finding, Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice reconstituted with WT pTreg cells still developed intestinal pathology and elevated serum IgE levels comparable to those present in untreated Atg16l1ΔCD4 littermates (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological and ELISA data shown in Figures 5F-H.

claim: Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice reconstituted with WT pTreg cells had elevated serum IgE levels comparable to untreated Atg16l1ΔCD4 littermates.
source: Consistent with this finding, Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice reconstituted with WT pTreg cells still developed intestinal pathology and elevated serum IgE levels comparable to those present in untreated Atg16l1ΔCD4 littermates (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Levels of autophagy were significantly higher in Foxp3+ Treg cells compared to Foxp3- CD4+ T cells in WT mice, both constitutively and after TCR activation.
source: Indeed, in WT mice we found that levels of autophagy were significantly higher in Foxp3+ Treg cells compared to Foxp3- CD4+ T cells, both constitutively and after TCR activation (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC3 staining data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: In mixed bone marrow chimeras, the reconstitution of CD4+ T cells was severely hampered in the absence of functional autophagy.
source: In this setting, the reconstitution of CD4+ T cells was severely hampered in the absence of functional autophagy and this deficiency was most pronounced in the Treg compartment of the spleen and cLP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data from mixed BM chimeras shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: Atg16l1-deficiency decreases the ability of Foxp3+ Treg cells to compete with WT Treg cells in a cell-intrinsic manner.
source: confirming that Atg16l1-deficiency decreases the ability of Foxp3+ Treg cells to compete with WT Treg cells in a cell-intrinsic manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mixed BM chimera experiments.

claim: At around 5 months of age, Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice developed a severe spontaneous inflammatory disease characterized by progressive weight loss, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and leukocyte infiltration in multiple tissues.
source: Although Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice appeared normal in early life, at around 5 months of age they developed a severe spontaneous inflammatory disease characterized by progressive weight loss, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and leukocyte infiltration in multiple tissues (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by weight curves, organ images, and histology shown in Figures 6C-E.

claim: The gastrointestinal tract was particularly affected in aged Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice, with marked inflammation in the SI and colon.
source: The gastrointestinal tract was particularly affected in aged Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice, with marked inflammation in the SI and colon (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological data shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: Intestinal inflammation in aged Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice was characterized by massive accumulation of activated CD4+ T cells in the intestinal LP and mLN.
source: Intestinal inflammation in aged Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice was characterized by massive accumulation of activated CD4+ T cells in the intestinal LP and mLN (Figure 7A–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry data shown in Figures 7A-D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The cLP infiltrate in aged Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice contained a mixed population of TH1, TH17 and TH2 effector cells, with a significant increase in the frequencies of IL-13+ CD4+ TH2 cells.
source: The cLP infiltrate in aged Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice contained a mixed population of TH1, TH17 and TH2 effector cells, with a significant increase in the frequencies of IL-13+ CD4+ TH2 cells (Figure 7E,F)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claim: The TH2 bias was not present in young Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice.
source: although this TH2 bias was not present in young Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Increased frequencies of Gata3+ CD4+ T cells were observed in the spleen, mLN and cLP of aged Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice.
source: In addition, we observed increased frequencies of Gata3+ CD4+ T cells in the spleen, mLN and cLP of aged Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Aged Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice had significantly elevated levels of circulating IgE and IgA.
source: Analyses of humoral responses in aged Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice revealed significantly elevated levels of circulating IgE and IgA, however IgG1 levels were not increased (Figure 7H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 7H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: IgG1 levels were not increased in aged Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice.
source: Analyses of humoral responses in aged Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice revealed significantly elevated levels of circulating IgE and IgA, however IgG1 levels were not increased (Figure 7H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 7H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Selective ablation of Atg16l1 in Foxp3+ Treg cells led to intestinal inflammation characterized by accumulation of all TH effector types, with a disproportionate increase in TH2 responses in aged mice.
source: Thus, selective ablation of Atg16l1 in Foxp3+ Treg cells led to intestinal inflammation that was characterized by accumulation of all TH effector types, with a disproportionate increase in TH2 responses in aged mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of effector T cell populations in Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice.

claim: The breadth and magnitude of TH2-associated responses were less pronounced in Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice compared to those observed in Atg16l1ΔCD4 mice.
source: However, the breadth and magnitude of TH2-associated responses were less pronounced in Atg16l1ΔFoxp3 mice compared to those observed in Atg16l1ΔCD4﻿ mice.
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion drawn from the data in both mouse models.

claim: Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells had comparable expression of pro-apoptotic (Bim, Bax) and anti-apoptotic (Bcl2) genes as control Treg cells.
source: Analyses of key regulators of apoptosis revealed that Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells isolated from spleen and cLP had comparable expression of pro-apoptotic (Bim, Bax) and anti-apoptotic (Bcl2) genes as those isolated from control mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells had higher expression of glycolytic genes than control Treg cells.
source: Analyses of genes involved in glycolysis, fatty acid synthesis (FAS) and fatty acid oxidation (FAO), revealed that Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells had higher expression of glycolytic genes, including Glut1, Slc16a3, Tpi1, Ldh-a, Aldo-a, Gpi1 and Pgk1, than control Treg cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The augmented glycolytic signature was much more pronounced in Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells isolated from cLP versus those from the spleen.
source: Strikingly, this augmented glycolytic signature was much more pronounced in Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells isolated from cLP versus those from the spleen (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data comparing spleen and cLP shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Expression of many key genes involved in FAS/FAO was markedly decreased in Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells.
source: Conversely, expression of many key genes involved in FAS/FAO, including Acc1, Acc2, Srebf1, Srebf2, Fdft1, Fabp1, Fabp4 and Fabp5 was markedly decreased in Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: WT cLP Treg cells showed increased FAS/FAO gene expression compared to their spleen counterparts.
source: Again, these differences were most pronounced in the intestine; WT cLP Treg cells showed increased FAS/FAO gene expression compared to their spleen counterparts, whereas Atg16l1-deficient cLP Treg cells were not able to up-regulate the expression of FAS/FAO genes (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data comparing spleen and cLP shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Atg16l1-deficient cLP Treg cells were not able to up-regulate the expression of FAS/FAO genes.
source: Again, these differences were most pronounced in the intestine; WT cLP Treg cells showed increased FAS/FAO gene expression compared to their spleen counterparts, whereas Atg16l1-deficient cLP Treg cells were not able to up-regulate the expression of FAS/FAO genes (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Atg16l1-deficiency profoundly influenced the expression of metabolic genes in intestinal Treg cells, with an altered balance of glycolytic and FAS/FAO gene expression.
source: Thus, Atg16l1-deficiency profoundly influenced the expression of metabolic genes in intestinal Treg cells, with an altered balance of glycolytic and FAS/FAO gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the qPCR data on metabolic gene expression.

claim: Treg cells isolated from the cLP showed markedly increased lipid uptake in comparison to mLN or spleen Treg cells.
source: Further evidence of increased reliance on lipid metabolism by colonic Treg cells was provided by our observation that Treg cells isolated from the cLP showed markedly increased lipid uptake in comparison to mLN or spleen Treg cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BODIPY C-16 uptake assays shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Colonic Treg cells showed increased expression of CD36 compared to splenic and mLN Treg cells.
source: A similar pattern was observed when we assayed expression of CD36, a fatty acid translocase that enhances FA uptake: colonic Treg cells showed increased expression of CD36 compared to splenic and mLN Treg cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells showed comparable levels of lipid uptake and CD36 expression as their autophagy-sufficient counterparts.
source: Interestingly, we found that Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells showed comparable levels of lipid uptake and CD36 expression as their autophagy-sufficient counterparts (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: Autophagy does not affect lipid uptake per se but rather affects lipid metabolism.
source: suggesting that autophagy does not affect lipid uptake per se but rather affects lipid metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparable lipid uptake but altered metabolic gene expression.

claim: Cell-intrinsic autophagy is indispensable for Foxp3+ Treg cell maintenance and function in peripheral tissues, particularly to suppress inflammatory responses within the gastrointestinal tract.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that cell-intrinsic autophagy is indispensable for Foxp3+ Treg cell maintenance and function in peripheral tissues, particularly to suppress inflammatory responses within the gastrointestinal tract.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Treg-specific deletion experiments and phenotypic analyses.

claim: Decreased survival of Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells was associated with an altered metabolic profile.
source: Decreased survival of Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells was associated with an altered metabolic profile, suggesting that autophagy plays an integral role in facilitating the metabolic adaptions required for long-term Treg cell survival in the intestine.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between survival defects and metabolic changes.

claim: Autophagy plays an integral role in facilitating the metabolic adaptions required for long-term Treg cell survival in the intestine.
source: Decreased survival of Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells was associated with an altered metabolic profile, suggesting that autophagy plays an integral role in facilitating the metabolic adaptions required for long-term Treg cell survival in the intestine.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the metabolic and survival data.

claim: Atg16l1-deficient naïve CD4+ T cells exhibited increased cell size compared with naïve CD4+ T cells isolated from Atg16l1fl/fl littermates.
source: Evidence that this might be the case came from our observation that Atg16l1-deficient naïve CD4+ T cells exhibited increased cell size compared with naïve CD4+ T cells isolated from Atg16l1fl/fl littermates (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Atg16l1-deficient naïve CD4+ T cells exhibited significantly increased OCR and ECAR.
source: We found that Atg16l1-deficient naïve CD4+ T cells exhibited significantly increased OCR and ECAR, metabolic changes that are typically observed in activated CD4+ T cells and are associated with increased aerobic glycolysis (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Seahorse metabolic flux analyzer data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3B.

claim: TH2 cells were larger than Treg cells.
source: We found that TH2 cells were larger than Treg cells, expressed higher levels of c-Myc, a critical regulator of metabolic reprograming in activated T cells, and had markedly higher ECAR, all indicative of enhanced aerobic glycolysis (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry and metabolic data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3C-E.

claim: TH2 cells expressed higher levels of c-Myc than Treg cells.
source: We found that TH2 cells were larger than Treg cells, expressed higher levels of c-Myc, a critical regulator of metabolic reprograming in activated T cells, and had markedly higher ECAR, all indicative of enhanced aerobic glycolysis (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3C-E.

claim: TH2 cells had markedly higher ECAR than Treg cells.
source: We found that TH2 cells were larger than Treg cells, expressed higher levels of c-Myc, a critical regulator of metabolic reprograming in activated T cells, and had markedly higher ECAR, all indicative of enhanced aerobic glycolysis (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Seahorse metabolic flux analyzer data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3C-E.

claim: Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells showed higher expression of c-Myc, significantly increased levels of ECAR and OCR, and were larger than their control Atg16l1-sufficient counterparts.
source: Furthermore, while Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells showed higher expression of c-Myc, significantly increased levels of ECAR and OCR, and were larger than their control Atg16l1-sufficient counterparts, we observed constitutively high and comparable levels of glycolysis in Atg16l1-deficient and Atg16l1-sufficient TH2 cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry and metabolic data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3C-E.

claim: Constitutively high and comparable levels of glycolysis were observed in Atg16l1-deficient and Atg16l1-sufficient TH2 cells.
source: Furthermore, while Atg16l1-deficient Treg cells showed higher expression of c-Myc, significantly increased levels of ECAR and OCR, and were larger than their control Atg16l1-sufficient counterparts, we observed constitutively high and comparable levels of glycolysis in Atg16l1-deficient and Atg16l1-sufficient TH2 cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metabolic data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3C-E.

claim: TH2 cells showed high expression of a panel of glycolytic genes irrespective of their Atg16l1 genotype.
source: These patterns were recapitulated when expression of key metabolic genes were analyzed; TH2 cells showed high expression of a panel of glycolytic genes irrespective of their autophagy Atg16l1 genotype, whereas Treg cell expression of glycolytic genes was generally lower, unless the Treg cells were autophagy-deficient (Figure 8—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3F.

claim: Treg cell expression of glycolytic genes was generally lower, unless the Treg cells were autophagy-deficient.
source: These patterns were recapitulated when expression of key metabolic genes were analyzed; TH2 cells showed high expression of a panel of glycolytic genes irrespective of their autophagy Atg16l1 genotype, whereas Treg cell expression of glycolytic genes was generally lower, unless the Treg cells were autophagy-deficient (Figure 8—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3F.

claim: The enhanced glycolytic metabolism constitutively employed by TH2 cells makes them more resistant to the metabolic changes that occur in the absence of autophagy.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the enhanced glycolytic metabolism constitutively employed by TH2 cells makes them more resistant to the metabolic changes that occur in the absence of autophagy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative metabolic analyses of TH2 and Treg cells.
